source_text:
Multa praetereo consulto: nam et haec nimis multa sunt, quae aut omnia aut pleraque [omnium] uera declarat ipsius prauae religionis obscuritas.
cur etenim occultare et abscondere quicquid illud colunt magnopere nituntur, cum honesta semper publico gaudeant, scelera secreta sint? cur nullas aras habent, templa nulla, nulla nota simulacra, numquam palam loqui, numquam libere congregari, nisi illud, quod colunt et interprimunt, aut puniendum est aut pudendum?
unde autem uel quis ille aut ubi deus unicus, solitarius, destitutus, quem non gens libera, non regna, non saltem Romana superstitio nouerunt?
Iudaeorum sola et misera gentilitas unum et ipsi deum, sed palam, sed templis, aris, uictimis caerimoniisque coluerunt, cuius adeo nulla uis nec potestas est, ut sit Romanis numinibus cum sua sibi natione captiuus.
at iam Christiani quanta monstra, quae portenta confingunt! Deum illum suum, quem nec ostendere possunt nec uidere, in omnium mores, actus omnium, uerba denique et occultas cogitationes diligenter inquirere : discurrentem scilicet atque ubique praesentem molestum illum uolunt, inquietum, inpudenter etiam curiosum, siquidem adstat factis omnibus, locis omnibus intererrat, cum nec singulis inseruire possit per uniuersa districtus nec uniuersis sufficere in singulis occupatus.
thought_title: The hidden God and the busybody God
orientation: Caecilius is still attacking Christianity, now arguing that its secrecy proves its shamefulness and that its one God is either unknown, captive, or an impossible busybody.
pass_a_gloss: Many things I pass over on purpose: for also these things are too many, which either all or most of all the very obscurity of their depraved religion declares true. For why do they strive greatly to hide and conceal whatever it is they worship, when honorable things always rejoice in public, crimes are secret? Why do they have no altars, no temples, no known idols, never to speak openly, never to assemble freely, unless that which they worship and suppress is either to be punished or to be ashamed of? But whence or who is he or where is the one god, solitary, destitute, whom no free people, no kingdoms, not even Roman superstition has known? The alone and wretched nation of the Jews worshipped one god, and they themselves, but openly, but with temples, altars, victims and ceremonies, whose force and power is so none that he is captive to the Roman deities with his own nation. But now what monsters, what portents the Christians invent! That their god, whom they can neither show nor see, diligently inquires into the habits of all, the acts of all, finally the words and hidden thoughts: running about of course and present everywhere, they want him troublesome, restless, shamelessly even curious, since he stands by all deeds, wanders among all places, when he can neither serve individuals, distracted through the universe, nor suffice for all, occupied in individuals.

choices.why: Glossary term; Caecilius uses it of Roman traditional worship, which he here treats as a known and established system.
Glossary term for simulacrum; Caecilius notes Christians have no known images of their god.
Keeps the triple adjective as a mocking description of the Christian God as alone and abandoned.
Glossary term for numen; Caecilius contrasts the Jewish god's weakness with Roman divine powers.
Preserves the adverbial force and the mocking tone of the accusation that God is a busybody.
Keeps the literal sense of being pulled apart or stretched thin by attending to everything at once.

pass_b_english: I pass over much of this on purpose, for even these charges are too many, and the obscurity of this depraved religion itself proves that all or most of them are true. Why else do they strive so hard to hide and conceal whatever it is they worship, when what is honorable always rejoices in the open, and crimes are secret? Why do they have no altars, no temples, no known idols, never speak in public, never assemble freely, unless what they worship and suppress is either punishable or shameful?

And whence is he, who is he, and where is he? This one god, solitary, destitute, whom no free people, no kingdom, not even Roman superstition knows. Only the Jews, a single wretched nation, also worshiped one god, but openly, with temples, altars, victims, and ceremonies. Yet his power and might are so nonexistent that he is a captive, along with his own nation, to the Roman deities.

But what monsters, what portents the Christians invent! They claim that their god, whom they can neither show nor see, diligently investigates everyone's character, everyone's actions, and finally everyone's words and hidden thoughts. They want him, you see, to be a busybody, always running about and present everywhere, restless, shamelessly even curious, since he stands by every deed and wanders through every place, though he cannot attend to individuals while stretched thin across the universe, nor be sufficient for the universe while occupied with individuals.

problems.quote: where does this god come from
problems.source_quote: unde autem uel quis ille aut ubi deus
problems.why: 'unde' means 'from where' in sense of origin/source, but 'quis' is 'who', 'ubi' is 'where'. The English 'where does this god come from' captures 'unde' but loses 'quis ille' (who is he).
problems.fix: And whence is he, who and where is this god...
problems.ruling: Latin asks both 'who is he' and 'where' but English only asks origin, omitting identity.

edits.old: And where does this god come from, who is he, and where is he—this one god, solitary, destitute, whom no free people, no kingdom, not even Roman superstition knows?
edits.new: And whence is he, who is he, and where is he—this one god, solitary, destitute, whom no free people, no kingdom, not even Roman superstition knows?

fixed: Changed 'where does this god come from' to 'whence is he' to capture 'unde' more precisely while keeping 'quis ille' (who is he) and 'ubi' (where is he) intact.

problems.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
problems.why: Octavius suddenly calls Caecilius 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks it's a new person.
problems.fix: Add note that Natalis is Caecilius's cognomen.

problems.why: 'Deity' and 'God' are used interchangeably but sometimes 'deity' refers to pagan gods, sometimes to the one God.
problems.fix: Distinguish pagan 'deities' from the one 'God' more consistently.

problems.quote: This one god, solitary, destitute, whom no free people, no kingdom, not even Roman superstition knows
problems.why: 'destitute' applied to God is odd; may mean 'forsaken' or 'neglected' but reads as God being poor.

problems.quote: they want him, you see, to be a busybody
problems.why: 'busybody' is too colloquial and comic for the theological argument about divine omnipresence.

edits.old: This one god, solitary, destitute, whom no free people, no kingdom, not even Roman superstition knows.
edits.new: This one god, solitary, forsaken, whom no free people, no kingdom, not even Roman superstition knows.

edits.old: They want him, you see, to be a busybody, always running about and present everywhere, restless, shamelessly even curious,
edits.new: They want him, you see, to be a meddler, always running about and present everywhere, restless, shamelessly even curious,

fixed: The 'Natalis' problem is not in this section; no edit needed.
The 'deity'/'God' distinction problem is not in this section; no edit needed.
Source 'destitutus' means 'forsaken, abandoned, left alone' — 'destitute' in modern English primarily means impoverished, so 'forsaken' better conveys the source sense.
Source 'molestum' means 'troublesome, annoying, burdensome' — 'busybody' is too colloquial and comic; 'meddler' is more fitting for the theological argument.

last_rejected.quote: I pass over much of this on purpose
last_rejected.why: The English 'I' could mislead readers into thinking this is narrator Marcus speaking, but this is Caecilius's speech per work brief (section 10 = Caecilius). The Latin has no explicit 'I' marker; 'praetereo' is first person. In context, this is clearly Caecilius continuing his speech. However, the English 'I' without attribution could confuse. But the brief says sections 5-13,15 are Caecilius. The source begins with 'Multa praetereo consulto'—no speaker change. Given the dialogue format, readers should understand. Not a clear error.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin praetereo is 1st‑person singular; 'I' correctly reflects the verb, not a mistranslation.

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker's rhetorical questions and the description of the Christian God, making the flow of Caecilius's argument easier to follow aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
notes.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.
